ai_summary: Great Britain's wind generation currently stands at 13.4 GW, with Scotland contributing an estimated 4.2 GW, representing 41.6% of installed Scottish wind capacity. Underpinned by this strong renewable generation, Scottish carbon intensity has dropped to 0 gCO2/kWh, compared to 56 gCO2/kWh across the GB-wide system. However, grid transmission bottlenecks continue to limit the transfer of this zero-carbon power southward. So far today, 2,814 MWh of Scottish generation has been curtailed through the Balancing Mechanism, incurring constraint costs of about £107,647. Annualizing today's figures indicates an estimated total yearly curtailment cost of £39 million, which increases consumer electricity invoices across the UK by an estimated £0.14/MWh. To replace this trapped output, fossil-fuel plants elsewhere on the network have burned an estimated 534,660 cubic meters of gas, releasing an additional 985 tonnes CO2 into the atmosphere. This ongoing dynamic illustrates the financial and environmental penalties of transmission constraints, where zero-emission generation is paid to turn down while carbon-intensive generation is paid to fire up elsewhere.
